title: Albert Edward McKenzie VC
body: Albert McKenzie was a 19-year-old Able Seaman during the First World War, awarded the Victoria Cross following the Royal Navy's famous raid on Zeebrugge, Belgium, in 1918.

On 22-23 April 1918, McKenzie landed with his machine gun as part of a storming party advancing down the Mole, a huge stone breakwater, alongside his Commanding Officer, most of whose party was killed. McKenzie was severely wounded working his gun in an exposed position.

He was chosen by his own shipmates from HMS Vindictive, Iris and Daffodil to be awarded the VC, and received it from King George V at Buckingham Palace on 31 July 1918 - the first London sailor ever to receive the medal, and the first chosen by the votes of his comrades.
Tragically, having almost fully recovered from his wounds, McKenzie caught flu in the epidemic that swept Europe at the end of the war, and died in October 1918, aged just 19.

title: John "Jack" Cornwell VC
body: John Cornwell, known as Jack, is remembered for his gallantry at the Battle of Jutland in 1916, the biggest naval battle of the First World War.

Aged just 16, Boy Seaman Cornwell served on HMS Chester. After being mortally wounded by steel splinters, he pulled himself to his feet and waited quietly for orders at his gun as the battle continued around him. He was found there by medics after the action, the sole survivor at his gun.
He died three days later and was posthumously awarded the Victoria Cross - the third-youngest recipient of the VC ever.

Newham Sea Cadet Unit's cap tally reads 'JT Cornwell VC' rather than their ship's name, a special honour granted by King George VI in 1942. The Cornwell Medal, one of the Sea Cadets' national awards, is named after him and given annually to the top-scoring cadet on the Petty Officer Cadet Advancement course.

title: Royal Marine Matthew Croucher GC
body: L/Cpl Matthew Croucher became one of only 20 living George Cross holders when the Queen awarded him the medal in October 2008.

Serving in Helmand, Afghanistan in February 2008, Croucher set off a trip-wire booby-trap that released a grenade. With less than seven seconds to react, he shouted a warning to three fellow Marines, dived to the ground, and used his backpack - containing a rocket, a battery and medical kit - to shield the blast.
He was thrown through the air by the explosion but suffered only a nosebleed. 'It was a case of either having four of us as fatalities or badly wounded, or one,' he later said.
The George Cross is the highest award for bravery not in the face of the enemy, surpassed only by the Victoria Cross itself.

title: William Job Maillard VC
body: William Job Maillard was a 35-year-old Royal Navy medical officer serving during the 1898 Occupation of Crete, when Britain joined France, Italy and Russia to expel Turkish forces from the island.

On 6 September 1898 at Candia in Crete, Maillard's ship HMS Hazzard sent parties to help release a besieged garrison. When a wounded seaman needed help, Surgeon Maillard - who had already found shelter - went back through heavy gunfire to rescue him.

He was awarded the Victoria Cross by Queen Victoria in December 1898, the first and only naval medical officer ever to receive it. His medal is on display at the Lord Ashcroft Gallery, Imperial War Museum, London.
